soil-phys-193.title: Advection, the river that carries what it holds
soil-phys-193.text: Dump ink into a river and it travels downstream as a pulse. The river's own current carries it, and that carrying has a name: advection, the transport of a substance or quantity by the bulk motion of a fluid. It needs currents, so it cannot happen in rigid solids. It also excludes the slow drift of molecules on their own, called diffusion. The ink does both at once, riding the current while it spreads, and the sum of the two is convection. Underground the same thing happens in {{ref:soil-phys-203}}. There advection carries contaminants along the main direction of flow at the seepage velocity, the speed at which water actually moves through the pores. Physicists write it as the advection equation, a first-order hyperbolic partial differential equation. It comes from a conservation law: whatever is transported is neither created nor lost along the way.

soil-phys-192.title: How pollution travels with moving groundwater
soil-phys-192.text: A spill on the surface can turn up years later in a distant well. Contaminant transport in groundwater is the movement of dissolved contaminants with the water flowing underground, and contaminant hydrogeology is the field that studies it, a branch of {{ref:soil-phys-208}}. Some contaminants are man-made, such as petroleum products, nitrate or radionuclides. Others are natural, such as arsenic or salinity. Three main mechanisms move them. {{ref:soil-phys-193}} carries them at seepage velocity. Diffusion spreads them from high to low concentration. Hydrodynamic dispersion spreads them further still. Diffusion and dispersion only spread a contaminant, though. Adsorption onto the soil does something different: it slows the contaminant's average velocity. Precipitation and decay also change what arrives. So the properties of the {{ref:soil-phys-201}}, beyond the flow itself, shape where pollution goes. Polluted groundwater forms a plume, and its advancing edge can reach wells and springs. Hydrologists track it with transport and groundwater models.

soil-phys-194.title: Why a contaminant plume spreads as it travels
soil-phys-194.text: Water cannot flow straight through soil. At every grain it must go left, right, up or down, so dissolved substances fan out around their average path. Hydrodynamic dispersion is this spreading of dissolved contaminants away from the mean path of the groundwater carrying them. It comes from small-scale unevenness in the porous medium and uneven water speeds through its {{ref:soil-phys-063}}. Over long distances a second effect takes over. Zones of higher and lower permeability offer preferential paths, like the {{ref:soil-water-157}} met earlier, and spread contaminants irregularly. Hydrologists measure the strength of dispersion with empirical numbers called dispersivities. Longitudinal dispersivity, αL, covers solute running ahead of or behind the mean flow. Transverse dispersivity, αT, covers solute drifting to the sides. These numbers hide a surprise. They stand in for details a large-scale model averages away, such as thin gravel or clay beds in sand. Dispersivity is partly a measure of missing information. That is why it is often said to depend on scale: dispersivity through 1 m3 of aquifer differs from that through 1 cm3 of the same material. Salinity models still need it as a soil input, alongside water retention and unsaturated hydraulic conductivity.

soil-phys-196.title: Retardation: when soil holds a pollutant back
soil-phys-196.text: Some contaminants move hundreds or thousands of times slower than the water around them. The reason is retardation by adsorption: a contaminant clings to soil surfaces, so its average movement lags behind the groundwater. A retardation factor measures how much. The idea mirrors the retardation factor of chromatography. Adsorption holds the contaminant back until the soil has taken up the amount set by the adsorption equilibrium. Only then does the front move on with the flow. Less soluble contaminants are held most strongly, so in practice only the more soluble species travel far. This is the one process in {{ref:soil-phys-192}} that slows a plume rather than spreading it. The factor is not a fixed number for a pollutant. It depends on the chemistry of both the contaminant and the aquifer, and it modifies the carrying done by {{ref:soil-phys-193}}.

soil-phys-195.title: Molecular diffusion, fast over millimeters, slow over meters
soil-phys-195.text: Double the distance and diffusion takes four times as long. Molecular diffusion is the random thermal movement of molecules that carries solutes from high to low concentration in the {{ref:soil-found-079}}. Over small distances it matters, but it spreads solutes slowly over large ones. Its coefficient is small and often negligible, except where groundwater barely moves, as in clay aquitards. Diffusion is a real physical process. Dispersion is an empirical factor that merely shares its mathematical form.

soil-phys-197.title: One equation for drifting and spreading
soil-phys-197.text: Most soil models describe salt on the move with one equation. The convection–diffusion equation, also called the advection–diffusion or scalar transport equation, tracks a quantity moved by both diffusion and {{ref:soil-phys-193}}. It is a parabolic partial differential equation built on the continuity equation, which keeps account of what enters and leaves. Diffusive flux comes from {{ref:soil-phys-181}} as −D∇c; advective flux is vc. A source or sink term R adds or removes the quantity, as when a chemical reaction creates or destroys a species. In porous media, v is the superficial velocity. SWAP, DrainMod-S, UnSatChem and Hydrus all couple the {{ref:soil-water-238}} with it, moving salts by advection and dispersion.

soil-phys-200.title: Dye tracing, following water with color
soil-phys-200.text: Dye traces showed karst groundwater moving 0.8 to 11.3 km a day. Dye tracing tracks a flow by adding dye to the water. It can be qualitative, proving a connection exists, or quantitative, with fluorometers measuring how much dye arrives. Fluorescein, developed in 1871, and its sodium salt uranine remain among the best tracers, alongside rhodamine, pyranine and sulforhodamine B. Organic matter, other chemicals, sunlight and acidic water weaken them. The traces also proved that models assuming uniform porosity do not fit karst aquifers.

soil-phys-199.title: Vadose zone models: solute transport on a computer
soil-phys-199.text: Hydrus, SWAP, DrainMod-S and UnSatChem all solve the same pair of equations. These vadose zone transport models simulate water flow and solute transport in unsaturated soil by solving the {{ref:soil-water-238}} numerically. Most join it to the {{ref:soil-phys-197}} to move salts. Hydrus needs soil hydraulic parameters for the water retention and unsaturated conductivity functions, plus starting and boundary conditions. Its one-dimensional version, HYDRUS1D, is available online and is used to estimate groundwater recharge.

soil-phys-198.title: Colloids, the hitchhikers that carry pollutants far
soil-phys-198.text: Plutonium at the Nevada Nuclear Test Site may have traveled far on tiny passengers. In colloid-facilitated transport, colloidal particles carry contaminants through surface water and groundwater. Radionuclides, heavy metals and organic pollutants sorb easily onto suspended colloids. These may be inorganic, such as clays and iron oxy-hydroxides, or organic, such as humic and fulvic substances. How far they move depends on soil structure, compaction and particle size. Compacted bentonite and deep clay ultrafilter them. The process drew real attention only in the 1980s.

soil-phys-177.title: Albedo, how much sunlight a surface sends back
soil-phys-177.text: Fresh snow reflects 0.80 of the sunlight that strikes it; bare soil reflects 0.17. That fraction is albedo, measured from 0 for a surface that absorbs everything to 1 for one that reflects everything. Desert sand scores 0.40, deciduous forest 0.15 to 0.18. Dark, low-albedo surfaces absorb most radiation. When snow melts off grass or soil, the darker ground warms the area and speeds further melting, a positive feedback that touches {{ref:soil-phys-137}}. Farming, deforestation and urbanization change the albedo of large areas.

soil-phys-180.title: Microclimate, the weather of a few meters
soil-phys-180.text: A valley bottom can frost sooner than the slope above it, because cold air sinks. A microclimate is a set of local conditions near the surface that differs persistently from its surroundings. It covers the air just above and the shallow soil and water below. It spans a few meters to at most a few kilometers. Moist soils damp temperature swings, while soils that dry easily swing more each day, and clay-rich soils keep heat and moisture near the ground. Farmers shape microclimate with irrigation, shading, windbreaks and vegetation.

soil-phys-181.title: Fick's laws: diffusion in two lines
soil-phys-181.text: In 1855 Adolf Fick put diffusion into two laws. The first, J = −D dφ/dx, says the diffusive flux J is proportional to the concentration gradient. D, the diffusion coefficient, has units of area per time. The second, ∂φ/∂t = D ∂²φ/∂x², says how concentration changes with time; it has the same form as the {{ref:soil-phys-183}}. Fick's law parallels Darcy's law for water and {{ref:soil-phys-182}}, and models transport in porous soils. Where porous media break these laws, diffusion is called non-Fickian.

soil-phys-179.title: Ice segregation, the real force behind frost heave
soil-phys-179.text: Freezing water expands, yet that is not what lifts most frozen ground. Most frost heaving and bedrock fracture in cold regions comes from ice segregation. In this process moisture moving through soil or rock collects in one zone and grows into {{ref:soil-phys-154}}s that wedge the material apart. It needs permeable soil or porous rock, temperatures at which ice and premelted water coexist, and a temperature gradient. With plenty of water one lens thickens until the heat released by freezing slows it. With little, new lenses form below. High overburden pressure or warm surfaces prevent it entirely.

soil-phys-185.title: Seasonal frost, ground that freezes and thaws each year
soil-phys-185.text: Each winter some ground freezes and each spring it thaws. This seasonal frost is one of three kinds of frozen ground classed by how long they stay frozen, beside permafrost and pereletok. Its repeated freezing and thawing pushes larger stones toward the surface, building patterned ground such as polygons. Cryogenic earth hummocks, formed by granular convection, appear here as well as in permafrost. Builders take note: rigid retaining-wall footings must sit below the seasonal frost depth, the reach of the {{ref:soil-phys-158}}.

soil-phys-184.title: Thermal effusivity, a material's resistance to temperature swings
soil-phys-184.text: Air scores 0.006 kJ/(m2·K·s½); water scores 1.6. Those numbers measure thermal effusivity, a material's ability to exchange heat with its surroundings. It equals the square root of thermal conductivity times volumetric heat capacity. Soil ranges from 0.5 to 2.6, dry sand 0.63. Effusivity measures thermal inertia. A low value means large daily temperature swings. A high one means much smaller swings. {{ref:soil-phys-164}} sets how fast a body reaches equilibrium; effusivity sets how well it resists periodic change. In remote sensing, a surface's thermal inertia reveals particle size, rock abundance, bedrock outcrop and induration.

soil-phys-182.title: Fourier's law: heat runs downhill in temperature
soil-phys-182.text: Heat always flows from warmer to cooler. Fourier's law, the law of heat conduction, puts a number on it. Heat flow through a material is proportional to the negative temperature gradient and to the area crossed. In one dimension, q = −k dT/dx, where k is the {{ref:soil-phys-141}}. Heat flux is in W/m2, k in W/(m·K), the gradient in K/m. The conductivity can change with temperature, with direction in anisotropic materials and with place in non-uniform ones. {{ref:soil-phys-181}} are its chemical analogue; Ohm's law is its electrical one.

soil-phys-183.title: The heat equation, temperature changing through time
soil-phys-183.text: In 1822 Joseph Fourier wrote an equation for how temperature in a body changes as heat spreads. The heat equation says a point heats or cools at a rate proportional to how much hotter or cooler its surroundings are. In three dimensions it reads ∂u/∂t = α(∂²u/∂x² + ∂²u/∂y² + ∂²u/∂z²). Here α is the {{ref:soil-phys-164}}, combining thermal conductivity, specific heat and density. Where a medium is not homogeneous and isotropic, α varies with position and the equation changes slightly.

soil-phys-178.title: Ground source heat pumps, tapping the steady earth
soil-phys-178.text: A few meters down, the seasons blur. A ground source heat pump heats and cools buildings by moving heat to or from the ground, whose temperature stays nearly constant through the year. Down to about 8–20 m, surface swings fade exponentially and lag about 6 months behind, an example of {{ref:soil-phys-142}}. Annual cycles reach 18.0 m in wet clay but only 4.5 m in dry sand. Loops in wet ground work better, because water conducts and stores heat well. Horizontal loops lie below the frost line, and efficiency typically reaches a coefficient of performance of 3–6.

openers.solute-transport-in-soil: Whatever dissolves in soil water can travel, and groundwater carries it wherever it flows. Some of the trip is simple carrying by the moving fluid. Some is spreading, as molecules drift from high to low concentration and water threads unevenly around the grains. Soil can also hold a substance back by adsorbing it, or tiny colloidal particles can carry it farther than it would go alone. This chapter follows those processes from first principles to the equation that combines them. It ends with the tools used to watch and predict them: colored dyes added as tracers and computer models of unsaturated soil.

reviews.solute-transport-in-soil: Every contaminant in groundwater is moved by the same few processes. Advection carries it along at the seepage velocity, while diffusion and dispersion spread it around that path without changing its average speed. Adsorption alone slows the plume, so less soluble substances can lag hundreds or thousands of times behind the water. Colloids work the other way, letting radionuclides and metals travel farther. The convection–diffusion equation joins these processes, and models such as Hydrus couple it to the Richards equation, while dye traces test the predictions in the field.
